question: A developer updates five products and plans to call a save method once per product. What is the EF Core way?
options: Call `SaveChangesAsync()` after each property change, once for every product you modify
Call `db.Update(product)` for each product first, otherwise EF Core ignores changes to entities it loaded
Open a transaction manually around the five saves, because `SaveChangesAsync()` is not transactional on its own
Change the tracked entities, then call `SaveChangesAsync()` once
explanation: The context is a unit of work: tracked entities are compared with their snapshots and one `SaveChangesAsync()` applies every change in a transaction. Calling `Update` on entities the context already tracks is unnecessary, and saving per entity adds round trips and loses atomicity.

question: Why does `AddDbContext` register the context as scoped?
options: A context is a non-thread-safe unit of work, so each request needs its own
Scoped services resolve faster than singletons, and the context is resolved on almost every request
A singleton context could not read the connection string, which is bound per request from configuration
Transient services cannot be injected into minimal API handlers, so scoped is the only lifetime left
explanation: One request is one unit of work, and one context must never be used by concurrent operations; the scoped instance is disposed at the end of the request. A singleton context would be shared by every concurrent request, and its change tracker would grow for the life of the process; speed of resolution has nothing to do with it.

question: When does this code send SQL to the database? `var q = db.Products.Where(p => p.Price < 10); q = q.OrderBy(p => p.Sku); var list = await q.ToListAsync();`
options: Three times, once per line, because each LINQ operator runs its own query
On the `Where` line; the `OrderBy` and the list are then done in memory
Once, on `ToListAsync`, as one statement with the filter and the order
Never; EF Core reads the whole table at startup and filters it in memory
explanation: `Where` and `OrderBy` on an `IQueryable` only build an expression. The terminal operator `ToListAsync` makes EF Core translate the whole expression into one SQL statement. Thinking each line runs a query misses deferred execution: on an in-memory list the operators also wait until the sequence is enumerated, but then run in C# over the objects instead of in SQL (03/03).

question: A query contains `.Where(p => MySlugHelper.Normalize(p.Name) == slug)`, where `Normalize` is your own C# method. What does EF Core 10 do?
options: Loads every product, runs the filter in memory, and logs a client-evaluation warning
Throws at runtime, because it cannot translate the method to SQL
Translates the method body to SQL automatically by inspecting its compiled IL
Ignores the untranslatable filter and returns every product without an error
explanation: Since EF Core 3.0, client evaluation is allowed only in the final `Select`; anywhere else EF Core throws instead of silently loading the table. Loading and filtering in memory was the behavior of versions before 3.0, which old answers online still describe.

question: A handler runs `await Task.WhenAll(db.Products.CountAsync(), db.Categories.CountAsync())` on the injected context. What happens?
options: Both queries run in parallel on the same connection, which halves the response time
The second query waits automatically until the first completes, so it works but is not parallel
It works only on SQL Server with MARS enabled, and throws on every other provider
EF Core throws, because a second operation started before the first completed
explanation: A `DbContext` does not support parallel operations, and EF Core detects this with an `InvalidOperationException`; await the queries one after the other or use separate contexts. Expecting an automatic queue is the tempting misconception; parallel work needs one context per operation, for example from `IDbContextFactory`.

question: Your `Product` has `public string Sku { get; set; }` with nullable reference types enabled and no other configuration. What column does EF Core create?
options: A `NOT NULL` column with no length limit or unique index
A nullable column of unlimited length, because `string` is a reference type
A `NOT NULL` column limited to 255 characters, with a unique index on it
No column at all, because string properties need a `[Column]` attribute
explanation: With nullable reference types on, EF Core maps `string` to a required column and `string?` to an optional one. It does not invent a length or a unique index; those come from `HasMaxLength` and `HasIndex(...).IsUnique()` or attributes, which is why the lesson's model sets them explicitly.
